_README: Cross-indicator rules. Each rule combines several weak signals into one explained alert. The COMBINATIONS are team hypotheses built on the cited findings; they have not been clinically validated. A rule never raises 'critical'. Actions are operational suggestions for the crew, never prescriptions.

masked_fatigue.title: Masked fatigue: you feel alert, the reaction test disagrees
masked_fatigue.explanation: Sleep has been short for several nights and the reaction-time test is worse than your own baseline, yet you rate yourself as alert. Under chronic sleep restriction people are largely unaware of their growing performance deficits.
actions: Postpone critical operations (EVA, docking, piloting) or hand them to a rested crewmate.
Protect a full sleep opportunity tonight (8.5 h is the scheduled sleep period on NASA missions).
Repeat the reaction-time test after sleep to confirm recovery.
sources: Van Dongen et al., Sleep 26(2):117-126 (2003): subjects were largely unaware of increasing cognitive deficits. https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20040087752
Basner, Mollicone & Dinges, Acta Astronautica 69:949-959 (2011): PVT-B, lapse threshold 355 ms. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3197786
Barger et al., Lancet Neurology (2014): about 6 h of sleep per night in flight for 8.5 h scheduled. https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/595450

fever_beyond_adaptation.title: Temperature above your space-adapted baseline, with a faster heart rate
fever_beyond_adaptation.explanation: Your resting temperature is above what the normal in-flight rise explains, and your resting heart rate is up as well. Together these can be an early sign of infection or heat strain rather than adaptation.
actions: Measure temperature and heart rate again after 30 minutes of rest.
Check for other signs: skin lesions, sore throat, urinary symptoms, cough.
Keep exercise light until temperature is back in your expected band.
Tell the Crew Medical Officer and include it in the next report to Mission Control.
sources: Stahn et al., Scientific Reports 7:16180 (2017): resting core temperature about 1 °C higher in flight. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5701078/

sustained_stress_load.title: Sustained stress load: short sleep, lower mood, faster heart rate
sustained_stress_load.explanation: Several days of short sleep, a mood below your usual level and a raised resting heart rate point to a sustained stress load. Spaceflight stress is associated with weaker immune surveillance and reactivation of latent herpes viruses.
actions: Protect sleep and reduce workload where the schedule allows.
Watch for skin rashes or cold sores and report them.
sources: Rooney, Crucian, Pierson, Laudenslager & Mehta, Frontiers in Microbiology (2019): herpes viruses reactivated in more than half of Shuttle and ISS crew. https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2019/03/190316162211.htm
